title: JSX and rendering
summary: What JSX compiles to, the expression rules inside braces, fragments, what React renders for each kind of value, and how a render becomes a DOM update.

sections.title: JSX is function calls
sections.body:
JSX is syntax for creating **React elements**: plain objects that describe what to show. With the automatic runtime (React 17+), `

Hi

` compiles to a call like `jsx("h1", { className: "title", children: "Hi" })`, imported from `react/jsx-runtime` for you. An element is a cheap description, not a DOM node. A **component** is a function that returns elements. React calls your component, compares the result with the previous one and updates only the DOM that changed.

sections.title: The rules of JSX
sections.body:
- Return **one root**. Wrap siblings in a fragment `<>…`, or `` when you need a key. - **Close every tag**, including `` and `
`. - Attributes are **camelCase** DOM properties: `className`, `htmlFor`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`. `aria-*` and `data-*` keep their dashes. - `style` takes an **object**: `style={{ marginTop: 8 }}`; numbers become pixels for most properties. - Braces hold **expressions**, not statements. Use a ternary, `&&` or a variable instead of `if` or `for` inside JSX. - Lower-case tags are DOM elements; capitalised tags are components. `

sections.title: What renders for each value
sections.body:
Strings and numbers render as text. `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` render **nothing**. Arrays render each item (each needs a `key`). Plain objects throw "Objects are not valid as a React child".

The classic trap: `0` and `NaN` are numbers, so `{count && <Badge />}` renders the text `0` when `count` is 0. Compare explicitly: `{count > 0 && <Badge />}`.
sections.code:
{null}{undefined}{false}{true}

//

{0 && "items"}

//

0

{["a", "b"]}

//

ab

(warns: missing keys)

{{ a: 1 }}

// throws: objects are not valid as a React child

sections.title: Render, then commit
sections.body:
React work happens in two phases. In the **render** phase React calls your components to compute the new element tree; this must be pure (no DOM writes, no subscriptions, same output for the same props and state). In the **commit** phase React applies the minimal DOM changes, then runs effects.

A component re-renders when its state changes, when its parent re-renders (unless it is memoised and its props are unchanged), or when a context it reads changes. Re-rendering is not the same as touching the DOM: if the output is the same, the DOM is left alone.

pitfalls: Writing `class` instead of `className`, or `for` instead of `htmlFor`.
Rendering an object (for example a `Date`) directly; format it into a string first.
Using `{count && …}` with a number that can be 0.
Forgetting that a component name must start with a capital letter, or JSX treats it as an HTML tag.
Doing side effects (fetching, writing to the DOM, mutating outside variables) while rendering.

gotchas.question: Why does `<myButton />` not use your `myButton` component?
gotchas.answer: Lower-case JSX tags are treated as built-in elements, so React creates an unknown `<mybutton>` DOM element. Components must be capitalised.

gotchas.question:
What does `
{[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2)}
` show?
gotchas.answer: The text `246`: numbers in an array render side by side. React also warns that each child in a list should have a key.
